# PIPELINE — the z-image-turbo vertical slice

> **SUPERSEDED 2026-09-18 by [`IMAGE.md`](IMAGE.md)**, which is now the file
> to read first for this vertical — it carries the current state, the
> re-checked hypotheses and the priority list (stages I0, I1, …). This file
> stays as the record of how the slice was built (stages 1-10), the full
> model inventory, the validation rules, and the measured budget the I-stages
> price against. Nothing below has been re-measured since 2026-09-14: an
> image is **14.26 s**, the DiT is **94%** of it.

> **This file is rewritten, not appended.** It states where the pipeline is
> *now* and what happens next. History belongs in `TODO.md` (session
> handoffs) and `research/` (closed findings); if a paragraph here is about
> the past, it is in the wrong file. Keep it under ~200 lines — it earns a
> few more with each stage that closes, and loses them when a stage's detail
> moves to `research/`.

**Status**: **the target is met, and the block has no layout work left in it.**
`go run ./cmd/zimage -prompt "..."` writes a 1024x1024 PNG in **14.3 s** —
tokenizer, text encoder, 34 DiT blocks over eight denoising steps, VAE, PNG —
and reproduces diffusers' fp32 CPU pipeline to **2.2e-2** of the decoded image.
Two runs agree to 14.18 s and 14.34 s. Every weight is resident: 7.17 GB of
text encoder, 12.54 GB of transformer, 0.30 GB of VAE and 4.90 GB of
activations, 21.9 s to load, and then images cost only their own time.

Stage 9 took the last host arithmetic out of the denoising loop, the patch
embedder and the final layer: **59 ms of CPU a step to 5-10**. Stage 10 then
removed the two dispatches in the block that moved no information — `pack v`
and `narrow ctx`, each of them a tensor read back and written out in the shape
the next kernel wanted — by making them the *store instruction* of the kernel
above: **18 dispatches a block to 16**, 53.17 ms to **51.80**, an image 14.49 s
to **14.26**.

So the whole of what is left is the DiT's arithmetic. The DiT is **94% of an
image**, and inside a block it is 74% GEMM at 73-76% of the WMMA ceiling, 14%
attention and 12% elementwise. Nothing outside it is worth a percent.

**Target**: `prompt → PNG` for Z-Image-Turbo at 1024x1024, 8 steps, fp16.

Since I1 the *size* is a ceiling rather than a fixture — `pipeline.Options`
sizes the arenas, `pipeline.Run` takes a size per image — which moved no
arithmetic and so changes nothing below. `IMAGE.md` has it.

## Why this exists

Phase 1 — fifteen-plus sessions of microbenchmarks — ended 2026-09-13 with no
convergence criterion (`TODO.md` carries the argument). **The unit of work is
now "a thing that runs", not "an experiment":** a profiler chooses the
optimisation targets, the backlog does not. Stage 4 is what that looks like —
it went looking for the kernel `results/shapes.csv` said would win, found it
the *slowest* in the ladder once the weight and the launch order were what the
memory system wanted, and closed three backlog items on the way without ever
having gone looking for them.

## The model, as the checkpoint actually describes it

Read with `go run ./cmd/inspect models/Z-Image-Turbo/<part>`. These differ
from `bench/modelshapes.go`, which was transcribed from `config.json` by
hand and has gaps that change the arithmetic:

| | |
|---|---|
| DiT blocks | **34**, not 30 — 30 `layers` + 2 `context_refiner` + 2 `noise_refiner` |
| Width / heads | dim 3840, 30 heads, head_dim 128, `qk_norm` on `[128]` |
| Attention | four matrices `to_q`/`to_k`/`to_v`/`to_out.0`, each `[3840, 3840]`, **no biases** |
| FFN | SwiGLU: `w1`,`w3` `[10240, 3840]` gate/up, `w2` `[3840, 10240]` down |
| Modulation | `adaLN_modulation` `[15360, 256]` + bias per layer; chunks are scale_msa, gate_msa, scale_mlp, gate_mlp, the scales offset by one and the gates through tanh |
| RoPE | 3D, `axes_dims [32, 48, 48]`, `axes_lens [1536, 512, 512]`, theta 256 |
| Latents | 16 channels, patch size 2 — 1024x1024 is 128x128 latents is **4096 tokens** |
| VAE | Flux `AutoencoderKL`: `block_out_channels [128,256,512,512]`, 2 layers/block, GroupNorm(32), SiLU, mid-block attention, 8x upsample, scale 0.3611, shift 0.1159 |
| Text encoder | Qwen3-4B: 36 layers, hidden 2560, FFN 9728, GQA 32q/8kv, head_dim 128, vocab 151936 |
| Scheduler | `FlowMatchEulerDiscrete`, shift 3.0, 1000 train timesteps, 8 NFE |
| Topology | **three phases, three lengths**: noise refiners over the image tokens, context refiners over the caption, then the 30 layers over the two concatenated. The context refiners are `modulation=False` — no adaLN, no scale, ungated residuals |

Sizes: transformer 6.155 B **F32** on disk (24.62 GB); text encoder 4.022 B
and VAE 0.084 B, both **BF16**. As fp16 the three total **20.5 GB**, so the
whole pipeline is resident in 128 GB unified memory at once.

## Stages

| # | Stage | State | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Checkpoint loader | **done** | `safetensors/`, `cmd/inspect` |
| 2a | VAE decoder, CPU reference | **done** | `zimage/vae/`, validated stagewise against diffusers |
| 2b | VAE decoder, Vulkan | **done** | 10 shaders, 119 dispatches, 1024² in 5.6 s |
| 3a | DiT block, CPU reference | **done** | `zimage/dit/`, validated stagewise incl. RoPE and qk-norm |
| 3b | Attention, Vulkan, scalar | **done** | 4 shaders; 1.28 TFLOP/s, kept as the oracle |
| 3c | Attention on WMMA | **done** | 38.8 TFLOP/s = 70% of ceiling, 30.4x |
| 4a | The block as a graph | **done** | `GPUBlock`, 26 dispatches, 65.6 ms; §2.8 |
| 4b | Fuse the tail, fix `ff.w13` | **done** | 18 dispatches, **49.3 ms**; §2.4, §2.6 |
| 4c | 34 blocks | **done** | `GPUStack`, 3 weight banks, **1.60 s/step**, 12.8 s/image |
| 5a | Tokenizer | **done** | `zimage/tokenizer`, byte-level BPE, 20 cases id for id |
| 5b | Text encoder, CPU reference | **done** | `zimage/qwen`, 35 of 36 layers, **2.08 s**; `cmd/textenc` |
| 5c | Text encoder, Vulkan | **done** | 21 dispatches/layer, 2 banks, **57 ms**; the winning tile moves with T |
| 6 | Scheduler + driver | **done** | `zimage/pipeline`, `cmd/zimage`; **19.8 s per image**, 2.5e-2 against diffusers |
| 7 | VAE mid block on WMMA | **done** | attention **94x**, projections **449x**; decode 5.65 s → **3.62 s**, image → **17.8 s**; §7 |
| 8 | conv2d on WMMA | **done** | implicit GEMM, **12.4x**; decode 3.62 s → **876 ms**, image → **15.0 s**; §8 |
| 9 | Head and tail on the device | **done** | host per step **59 ms → 5-10 ms**, image → **14.5 s**; §9 |
| 10 | The layout passes as epilogues | **done** | 18 dispatches → **16**, image → **14.26 s**; §10 |

Each stage gets a CPU implementation in Go first: it separates "do I understand
the architecture" from "is the shader right", and once it matches diffusers it
is the oracle the GPU port is debugged against.

## The rule for every stage

Validate against the **library reference**, not against a shape table.
`reference/dump_vae.py` and `reference/dump_dit_block.py` are the pattern: run
a fixed input through diffusers in fp32 on CPU, dump **every submodule's
output**, and walk the graph stage by stage against it. Stage 5's oracle is
`transformers` rather than `diffusers` (`reference/dump_qwen.py`,
`reference/dump_tokenizer.py`) — same pattern, and it does one thing more:
where the port relies on an assumption about the library (which hidden state
`[-2]` is, whether padding changes an answer) the dump *measures* the
assumption and the test reads the number. `GPUBlock.RunTo` is
what makes that possible on an 18-dispatch graph whose intermediates are
overwritten before it ends: it re-runs the prefix up to a labelled dispatch.

Five rules around that, each of which has caught something:

- **A negative control per test**, deliberately breaking the implementation
  and asserting the break is caught. Without one the test proves only that it
  runs. `zimage/vae`'s land 141x-14000x above tolerance, stage 3c's 27x-569x,
  stage 4a's **1160x-15828x**.
- **When an optimisation removes a stage boundary, keep the slow path** and
  check the fast one against it at the last point its own output is visible.
  Stage 4b's fusions are bit-identical there; its fp16 store is not, and is
  measured separately for it rather than folded into one bound.
- **Normalise the error by the tensor's RMS**, not per element — but know what
  that costs: two of stage 4a's stages report 3e-2 where their worst element
  is 2e-3 of itself, because an RMS norm's output inherits the learned
  weight's dynamic range. Stage 5 is where that bill came due: Qwen3's
  massive activations put the absmax **109-238x** above the RMS, so the RMS
  alone fails a stage whose worst element is off by 9e-6 of itself. The
  denominator needs a floor — `max(|want|, rms)` per element — and **which
  denominator is right is a property of the model**, so look before
  inheriting one. Stage 6 needs a third answer: a denoising trajectory is
  chaotic, so it is bounded in **relative L2** over the whole tensor.
- **Validate the composition too, and do it at a small size.** Every stage's
  own oracle passed while the pipeline made a black image, because what was
  wrong was between them. `reference/dump_zimage_run.py` runs the whole
  diffusers pipeline in fp32 on the CPU at **256x256** — 3.2 s a step, the
  full eight steps and the VAE in half a minute — because the composition
  does not know how big the image is. It is the cheapest test in the project
  and it found three bugs in one sitting.
- **A real prompt is not a random tensor.** Two of stage 6's three bugs only
  appear on real inputs: SwiGLU's product overflows fp16 at 7.1e4 where the
  random fixture peaks at 5.1e4, and the VAE's watchdog cap only fails at the
  full image. Random-input validation is necessary and it is not sufficient.

## What the kernels already give us

Measured on this device (`research/`), and load-bearing for every stage:

- **fp16 is the fast path.** WMMA fp16 is 55.5 TFLOP/s; WMMA int8 is the
  *same* rate, not double (§0). The DiT's projections reach **42.0, 76%**.
- **Do not quantize the DiT for speed.** At M=4096 its intensity is `4*M` =
  16384 flop/byte against a 235 crossover, so it is compute-bound and 4-bit
  weights buy nothing (§3.4). Quantize for footprint only.
- **Coverage law** (§5.1b): achievable bandwidth is
  `min(1, C/gcd(stride, 4096))`, C being the contiguous run the in-flight
  requests hold. Land `gcd` in [128, 256] B. Getting this wrong costs 2-8x.
- **Order, twice.** Store every WMMA operand as 16x16 fragment tiles (§2.8) —
  free on a weight, 1.43-1.46x — and walk the grid in bands of 8 columns
  rather than rows (§2.4), which keeps the resident workgroups a *block* of C
  instead of a row that streams all of B past one A slab: **1.84x** on the one
  shape wide enough to suffer, and only 1.16x without the tiling. They are one
  lever measured in two places.
- **Both halves of the roofline are in this pipeline, and they want opposite
  kernels.** The DiT is compute-bound at 16384 flop/byte; the text encoder
  runs the same kind of layer at `T` flop/byte, which for a prompt is 8-512
  against the same 235 crossover. Measured: the encoder's winning tile is 16
  or 32 rows at 24 tokens, 64 at 128, and the DiT's own 128x256 at 256+ —
  1.24x for taking the DiT's default at a short prompt, 1.92x for taking the
  narrowest at a long one. Re-planning per run is free (`qwen.PlanFor`),
  because every rung reads the same staged weight.
- **Kernel choice is per shape only while something else is wrong.** The DiT's
  three shapes disagreed until both of the above were applied; then one kernel
  won all three. `results/shapes.csv`'s pick measures 23.5 s/image against
  13.4.
- **Time dispatches, not `Apply`** — but know which side of the heap you are
  on. A host read of the device-local host-visible arena runs at **0.18 GB/s**
  (writes: 29), so a wall-clock figure with a read-back in it is measuring the
  read-back. That heap's budget on this device is about **8 GB**, though, and
  `vk.NewBuffer` silently falls back to the plain host-visible one past it,
  where the same read runs at **15 GB/s** — so a single-stage benchmark and
  the 20.5 GB pipeline are on opposite sides of it and disagree by 83x on what
  a read-back costs. `cmd/bus` measures it; stage 9 found it.

## Measured baselines, per stage

The stage-level figures the budget above is made of. Each stage's own
measurement harness is still there — `cmd/ditstack`, `cmd/vaebench`,
`cmd/textenc -gpu` — and each stage's research note has the sweep behind it.

**The DiT** (`go run ./cmd/ditstack -image 4096 -caption 128`, GPU timestamps,
best of three, two runs agreeing to 51.78 and 51.82 ms a layer block):

| phase | blocks | tokens | per block | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `noise_refiner` | 2 | 4096 | 49.4 ms | 98.8 ms |
| `context_refiner` | 2 | 128 | 2.57 ms | 5.1 ms |
| `layers` | 30 | 4224 | **51.80 ms** | 1.55 s |
| **one step** | 34 | | | **1.66 s** |

A block is 16 dispatches: **74% GEMM** (37.97 ms), 14% attention (7.19 ms) and
12% elementwise (5.93 ms across eight passes). One kernel
(`wg128x256_bt16_swz8`) wins all three of its shapes at **40.6-42.0 TFLOP/s**,
73-76% of the ceiling. Residency is 12.54 GB in three fp16 banks of 4.25, 4.25
and 3.54 GB holding 12, 12 and 10 blocks, plus a 0.51 GB fp32 arena and 1.29 GB
of activations, against an 83.79 GiB device-local host-visible heap.

The layers phase measures 1.56 s of wall clock against 1.55 s of dispatches,
and in the pipeline a step is 1.67-1.70 s against the same 1.66 — 10 ms of
host and 9 of bus, and the ~50 ms remainder is the one thing in this budget
still unaccounted for (stage 9 ruled out submit batching for it).

**The VAE** (`go run ./cmd/vaebench`), every convolution and the mid block on
the matrix cores, wall clock including a read-back:

| latent | image | fp32 arena | fp16 arena | wall | before stage 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16² | 128² | 46 MB | 9 MB | 13 ms | 47 ms |
| 32² | 256² | 185 MB | 34 MB | 46 ms | 192 ms |
| 64² | 512² | 738 MB | 135 MB | 204 ms | 856 ms |
| 128² | **1024²** | 2.95 GB | 539 MB | **876 ms** | 3.62 s |

The wall column includes a read-back that the *pipeline* does not pay — 12.58
MB at the 0.18 GB/s a 3.5 GB program gets, 71 ms — which is why a decode costs
805 ms inside an image and 876 on its own (stage 9).

There is **no arithmetic left in this decoder**: conv3x3 is 244 ms at 41-42
TFLOP/s (30%) and the next four items are bandwidth-bound elementwise passes
running back to back over the same tensors — group norm 244 ms, the conv pack
160, SiLU 61, the adds 40, **63% together**. So what it wants next is not a
kernel but **fusion**, the same shape of change as stage 10: a SiLU whose only
consumer is a convolution could write the blocked fp16 form *instead of* its
fp32 output. ~200 ms of 805, and 1.4% of an image.

**The text encoder** (`go run ./cmd/textenc -gpu`), 35 layers, 7.07 GB of fp16
weights in two banks: **57.1 ms** at 24 tokens, 71.4 at 128, 170 at 512,
against 2.08 s and 9.17 s on the CPU. One run walks the roofline — the weights
are read once whatever T is, so GB/s of weight falling (124, 99, 42) *is*
GFLOP/s rising (3.0, 12.7, 21.2 T). 0.4% of an image; detail in
[`research/stage-5-text-encoder.md`](research/stage-5-text-encoder.md).

## Where the image budget stands

`go run ./cmd/zimage -width 1024`, wall clock, two runs agreeing to 14.18 s
and 14.34 s.

| | per image, 1024², 8 steps | share |
|---|---|---|
| denoising | **13.37 s** | 93.8% |
| — of which the 34 blocks | 13.3 s | 93.1% |
| — of which the host | 0.08 s | 0.6% |
| VAE decode | **0.81 s** | 5.7% |
| text encoder, 19 tokens | 0.06 s | 0.4% |
| caption refiners, once per image | 0.006 s | 0.04% |
| **total** | **14.26 s** | |

Loading is 21.9 s and happens once: 7.17 GB of text encoder, 12.54 GB of
transformer, 0.30 GB of VAE weights, 4.90 GB of activation arenas.

**The image is the DiT and nothing else.** Everything outside it — tokenizer,
text encoder, caption refiners, VAE, and now the head and tail — is 6.4%
together, and no item in it is worth more than 1.3%. There is no boundary work
left: the host does a patchify and an unpatchify on a megabyte, and the bus
carries 1 MB each way per step.

And inside the block there is no *layout* left either — stage 10 took the last
of it. Everything remaining is arithmetic or the traffic arithmetic needs:

- **The seven projections, 9.9 s an image (69%), at 73-76% of the WMMA
  ceiling.** The quarter they do not reach is 2.6 s, which is an order of
  magnitude more than everything else in this list together. It is also the
  hardest: stage 4 already applied the fragment-tiled weight (§2.8), the
  banded grid (§2.4) and the hoisted K-slab (§2.7), and the ablation behind
  `results/gemm_wmma.csv` is 1.25x behind what the pipeline already does.
- **Attention at 38 TFLOP/s**, 1.9 s an image, against the GEMMs' 40.6-42.0.
  Worth ~0.2 s if it caught up. Stage 10 halved its store and removed its LDS
  staging and neither moved it, which agrees with stage 3c that the register
  file is what binds it.
- **The eight elementwise passes, 5.93 ms a block and 1.6 s an image.** Each
  reads the residual stream and writes it; `swiglu` (1.45 ms) and the two
  gated residuals (0.89, 0.85) are half. Unlike stage 10's two they compute
  something, so what they want is fusion into a neighbour — and the neighbour
  is usually a GEMM, which is where §2.6 and stage 10 both ended.

Below those: the VAE's elementwise fusions are ~200 ms (1.4%) and the text
encoder's remaining 1.9x is worth less than a percent.

**One correction worth carrying**, because it sat at the top of this list for
four sessions: the layout item was priced here at "~1.0 s an image" and was
**~0.29 s**. The measurement it came from (stage 4) said 1.0 **ms a block**
and the unit was lost in transcription. A number quoted between documents
should carry the dimension it was measured in.

## What each stage found

One file per stage in `research/`, indexed in `research/README.md`. The ones
that are load-bearing for what is left:

- **[Stage 10, the layout epilogues](research/stage-10-layout-epilogues.md)**
  — the two dispatches in the block that moved no information, absorbed into
  the store of the kernel above: **18 a block to 16**, an image 14.49 s to
  14.26. Possible at all because in both cases the data was already in the
  right registers in the right 16x16 shape, so a transposed fragment tile is
  a *column-major `coopMatStore` of stride 16* and not a transpose. Two other
  things fell out: the item had been mispriced 3.4x by a units slip
  (`1.0 ms a block` quoted as `1.0 s an image`), and the old path was doing a
  **double rounding** — which is why 84 halves in 1.2 M of the context differ
  and why every one of them is an exact fp16 tie.
- **[Stage 2, the VAE](research/stage-2-vae-decoder.md)** — two hard device
  limits that still bind: 4.29 GB per storage buffer, and a reset watchdog
  that kills a multi-second command buffer. Its absmax survey (497 through the
  decoder, 1.16e7 in the mid block's scores) is what stages 7 and 8 narrowed
  against, and is now asserted by `TestConvInputsFitFP16`.
- **[Stage 3, attention](research/stage-3-dit-attention.md)** — 70% of the WMMA
  ceiling, but only once every operand is stored as fragment tiles. Three port
  hazards: RoPE pairs *adjacent* components, the q/k norms are *per head*, and
  v is the operand that needs transposing.
- **[Stage 4, the block](research/stage-4-dit-graph.md)** — 90.0 ms/block to
  **49.3**, none of it arithmetic. The interactions are the finding: the
  swizzle is worth 1.84x on a tiled weight and 1.16x on a row-major one, the
  hoisted K-slab becomes a *loss* on a tiled weight, and once all of it is
  applied the three shapes that disagreed on a kernel stop disagreeing.
- **[Stage 5, the text encoder](research/stage-5-text-encoder.md)** — **2.08 s
  to 57 ms**, and the encoder sits on the **memory-bound** half of the
  roofline, so unlike the DiT its winning kernel *moves with the prompt
  length* and re-planning per run is free. Three conventions invert between it
  and the DiT — NeoX RoPE, causal attention, grouped heads — and Qwen3's
  massive activations break an RMS-normalised error bound.
- **[Stage 6, the pipeline](research/stage-6-pipeline.md)** — every bug this
  stage had was in the *composition* and invisible to each component's own
  oracle: SwiGLU's product **overflows fp16 on a real prompt and never on a
  random one**, a new push constant on a shared shader silently zeroed the
  text encoder's feed-forward, and a dispatches-per-submit cap is a proxy for
  a time cap that stops being one when the dispatches differ 100x. Also: the
  context refiners take neither the timestep nor the latents, so **two of the
  three phases run once per image rather than once per step**.
- **[Stage 7, the VAE mid block](research/stage-7-vae-mid-block.md)** —
  attention **1.43 s → 15.1 ms**, the four projections **503 ms → 1.12 ms**.
  The finding that outlives the stage: this block's softmax is so saturated
  that a kernel **dropping three quarters of every dot product decodes the
  same image**, so no end-to-end tolerance can validate it.
- **[Stage 9, the head and tail](research/stage-9-head-and-tail.md)** — the
  host's share of a step **59 ms → 5-10 ms**. A bias and a *pad token* become
  extra columns of K, so `y = Wx + b` and `y = x_pad_token` come out of one
  biasless GEMM. And the correction that matters beyond this stage: the
  engine's "a host read-back runs at 0.2 GB/s" holds only below **~8 GB of
  allocation**, where `vk.NewBuffer` still gets the device-local heap; the
  20.5 GB pipeline reads the same arena **83x faster**, which is why the 0.8 s
  an image this stage was partly priced on was never there (`cmd/bus`).
- **[Stage 8, conv2d](research/stage-8-vae-conv.md)** — the last operator in
  the VAE, **3.02 s → 244 ms** at 41-42 TFLOP/s. The finding is the layout: a
  patch fragment is contiguous only if the **channel** axis is the tiled one,
  because tiling the pixel axis — what every other operand in this engine does
  — makes the `dw = ±1` window straddle two tiles. Also: §2.7's K-slab hoist
  does **nothing** once both operands are fully covered.
- **[Stage 4c, the stack](research/stage-4c-dit-stack.md)** — splitting a
  12.0 GB weight arena across storage buffers costs **one pipeline per bank
  and nothing per dispatch**; six banks are bit-identical to one.

1	# API — the models behind one HTTP server
2	
3	`cmd/serve` is the long-lived process: an OpenAI-shaped API over the models in
4	this repository, with one flag per vertical deciding what is resident.
5	
6	    go run ./cmd/serve -llm -embed -tts -stt
7	
8	`GOALS.md`'s last line — "we will ultimately serve up a HTTP API serving these
9	features, in Go" — is what this is, and all five verticals are now behind it.
10	
11	The same process has a **second door** for the two speech verticals, because
12	the thing on the other side of a house's microphones does not speak OpenAI:
13	
14	    go run ./cmd/serve -tts -stt -wyoming 0.0.0.0:10300
15	
16	See [Home Assistant speaks Wyoming](#home-assistant-speaks-wyoming-not-openai).
17	
18	## What answers today
19	
20	| Endpoint | State |
21	|---|---|
22	| `GET /v1/models` | **done** — lists what the process actually loaded, with the speech model's voices |
23	| `POST /v1/chat/completions` | **done** — qwen3.8-flash-next, `-llm`, buffered and SSE |
24	| `POST /v1/responses` | **done** — the same generation, OpenAI's newer envelope |
25	| `POST /v1/messages` | **done** — the same generation, Anthropic's envelope |
26	| `POST /v1/audio/speech` | **done** — kokoro, `-tts` |
27	| `POST /v1/audio/transcriptions` | **done** — parakeet, `-stt`, with word and segment timings |
28	| `POST /v1/embeddings` | **done** — Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, `-embed`, float or base64, MRL widths |
29	| `POST /v1/images/generations` | **done** — z-image-turbo, `-image`, any size the arenas hold, streaming previews with `-preview` |
30	| `POST /v1/images/edits` | **done** — SDEdit over the VAE's encoder, `-image -edits`, multipart or JSON |
31	
32	Every endpoint is *routed*, including the ones that are not implemented: a
33	client gets a 501 that says what is missing and, where a flag would have fixed
34	it, which flag. A 404 would mean a misspelled path and nothing else.
35	
36	## The three packages
37	
38	    cmd/serve   flags, load order, graceful shutdown
39	    backend/    the adapters: weights, device residency, one lock each
40	    api/        routing, request shapes, encoding; imports no model
41	
42	The direction of the dependency is `cmd/serve -> backend -> api`, never the
43	other way. `api` *declares* the backend interfaces (`api.SpeechBackend`,
44	`api.TranscriptionBackend`, `api.CompletionBackend`, `api.EmbeddingBackend`,
45	`api.ImageBackend`) and implements none of them, so it pulls in no checkpoint
46	loader and no Vulkan, and its tests run against fakes in milliseconds —
47	`go test ./api/` needs no `models/` directory and no GPU, including for the
48	three chat envelopes and their streams and for every size the image endpoint
49	resolves.
50	
51	What crosses the boundary is deliberately model-shaped and not
52	container-shaped. A speech backend returns `*audio.Clip` — samples and a rate
53	— and the HTTP layer encodes the WAV or the raw PCM, because which one was
54	asked for is the request's business and not the model's. A transcription
55	backend is handed an already-decoded clip for the same reason in reverse.
56	
57	**The completion backend's signature is a streaming one**, and the buffered
58	response is written in terms of it rather than the other way round. A token
59	on this part costs ~44 ms of the wall clock at 22.7 tok/s, so a 500-token
60	answer is 22 seconds: an interface that returned the whole thing would make
61	the streamed endpoint impossible to build on top of it, where the buffered one
62	is a string builder over the streaming one. That is also what keeps the two
63	answers to the same prompt identical — a server whose streaming path is a
64	separate implementation is a server whose two answers eventually differ, over
65	some whitespace one of them strips.
66	
67	## The log does not keep the conversations
68	
69	`-log-bodies` is off by default, and that default is the point: this server's
70	request and response bodies are its users' prompts and answers, and a process
71	that stays up would otherwise write every one of them to disk as a side effect
72	of having an access log. With it off the log still carries the method, the
73	path, the status, the duration and the sizes — which is what an operator reads
74	anyway. An event stream is never kept whatever the flag says: the first
75	kilobyte of one is a fragment of a frame.
76	
77	## Requests are serialised at the queue
78	
79	A `vk.Device` holds a single queue and nothing in `vk` is externally
80	synchronised, so two requests recording and submitting at once is undefined
81	behaviour rather than contention. `backend.Device` is the device plus the lock
82	that fixes that: every run and every staging pass goes through `Do`, and the
83	server is concurrent at the HTTP layer and serial at the GPU.
84	
85	That is also the only arrangement that makes sense on this part. These models
86	are each sized to saturate the iGPU; two of them interleaved would not go
87	faster, they would share a 236 GB/s bus.
88	
89	## Residency, and the one place it is not resident yet
90	
91	**The language model is resident, and it is most of the machine.** `-llm`
92	stages all 48 layers, the dense banks and the 512-expert bank at startup —
93	**33.5 s**, and the process then holds ~84 GB — so a request is a prefill and
94	one forward pass per token with no weight ever moving again. Two numbers are
95	decided at startup rather than per request: `-llm-ctx`, the attention cache's
96	cell count and so the longest conversation the process can hold, and
97	`-llm-batch`, how many tokens the prefill arenas hold. A conversation past the
98	cache is refused with both numbers rather than truncated at one end; a prompt
99	past the batch is prefilled in chunks of it, which is the same computation by
100	L7b's gate.
101	
102	**The device lock is taken per forward pass and not per request.** A
103	completion is seconds long and the speech models are milliseconds, so holding
104	the queue for a whole generation would make a transcription wait behind it for
105	nothing: between two decode steps there is no work in flight. What is held for
106	the length of a request is the *graph*, whose cache, PLE ring and DeltaNet
107	state are one sequence's — two conversations interleaved in them would not be
108	slower, they would be one conversation.
109	
110	**Parakeet is resident.** `-stt` stages the encoder and the transducer tail
111	once, sized for `-max-audio` seconds (60 by default), and every shorter clip
112	runs in the same arenas — `UploadMel` settles the geometry per run. A request
113	costs a front end on the host and two submits. A longer clip is refused with a
114	message saying what the server was sized for, rather than being truncated.
115	
116	**The embedding model is resident**, and it is the cheapest thing here:
117	`-embed` stages 0.88 GB of fp16 banks in **1.3 s**, and an input then costs
118	**11.5 ms** whatever it says — a 27-token query and an 8-token document take
119	the same time, because at these lengths the run is the weights read once
120	(EMBEDDING.md E6). `-embed-tokens` sizes the arenas and is therefore where an
121	input is truncated: the front of the text survives and the end-of-text token
122	is re-appended, because last-token pooling takes *that* row and an input
123	truncated through it would be pooled from an ordinary word.
124	
125	**The image pipeline is resident, and its resolution is not part of what is
126	resident.** `-image` stages 7.2 GB of text encoder, 12.5 GB of transformer and
127	0.3 GB of VAE in **21.2 s**, sizes 4.9 GB of activation arenas for
128	`-image-size`, and then a request moves no weight. That last clause is what
129	this endpoint needed and did not have: `zimage/pipeline` used to fix its width
130	and height at construction, so a size was a residency question.
131	
132	It is not one, and none of the three graphs had to change to stop it being
133	one. The transformer states its run length per upload (`GPUStack.Upload`,
134	which the caption phase has always used to run 32 rows in a 4128-row arena),
135	the VAE re-records its graph from the latent it is handed and checks the arena
136	rather than assuming it, and the rotary table is rebuilt per run anyway. So
137	`-image-size` became a *ceiling* and a default, the way `-max-audio` is for
138	parakeet, and every smaller image runs in the same arenas. Measured on one
139	1024x1024 process, two runs each:
140	
141	| size | image tokens | request |
142	|---|---|---|
143	| 1024x1024 | 4096 | **14.55 s** / 14.62 |
144	| 1024x576 | 2304 | 7.95 s |
145	| 512x512 | 1024 | **3.65 s** / 3.64 |
146	| 256x256 | 256 | 1.33 s |
147	
148	`-previews` adds 1.0 GB of arena to that and no measurable staging time —
149	24.9 GB becomes **25.9** — and the two processes render the same non-streamed
150	1024x1024 image in 14.64/14.72 s and 14.72/14.80. A preview decoder that is
151	not asked for costs residency and nothing else. `-edits` is the same bargain
152	one size up: 0.21 GB of encoder weights and 1.8 GB of arena at a 1024x1024
153	ceiling, and the encoder runs only on a request that carries a picture.
154	
155	**What bounds a request is each side, and not the area** — which is worth
156	stating because the plausible guess is the other one. A diffusion model's cost
157	is its token count, so the same area in another shape should be the same work,
158	and for the transformer it is: 512x2048 is the same 4096 rows as the square.
159	The decoder disagrees. Stage 8 gave it an fp16 arena of *blocked* copies of
160	each convolution's input, and a block is padded on each axis separately, so
161	redistributing the same area over a taller grid needs more arena than it has —
162	measured at 33 MB against 32. A run that got that far would fail in the VAE
163	after the whole denoising loop, so `pipeline.geomFor` refuses it at the door
164	and the endpoint refuses it before that. Both sides inside the ceiling makes
165	every tensor in all three graphs smaller elementwise, which is the condition
166	that actually holds; `zimage/pipeline`'s `TestSameAreaTallerShapeIsRefused` is
167	the measurement.
168	
169	**Kokoro is not.** Its arenas are sized for one utterance's frame count, and
170	the durations decide that, so nothing can be staged until the phoneme side has
171	run (SPEECH.md T2, T4c). `-tts-gpu` therefore stages *per request* — the
172	sequence `cmd/tts` uses, unchanged, because it is the one T4 and T6 measured —
173	and it is **off by default** until that cost is measured against the host
174	path, which is what `-tts` alone runs.
175	
176	Two things would fix it, and both are measurements rather than arguments:
177	
178	- **Bucketed residency.** Size the arenas above the utterance and zero-pad the
179	  alignment up to them, trimming the tail by `Prosody.Samples`. The phoneme
180	  side already accepts any frame count up to the one it was built for
181	  (`GPUPhonemes.sharedGraph`); whether the generator's stages tolerate the
182	  padding is the open question.
183	- **Skipping the second prosody pass.** The vocoder still reads `asr`, `f0`
184	  and `energy` from the host (SPEECH.md T7), so the host prosody that settles
185	  the length could feed the device vocoder directly and the phoneme side would
186	  not need staging at all.

240	## A second turn is a continuation
241	
242	A chat client re-sends the whole conversation every turn, so the naive server
243	prefills ten turns of history to answer the tenth. This one does not: the
244	adapter keeps the token sequence the graph is holding, and when a request
245	continues it — the same tokens, plus more — the new tokens are `Extend`ed onto
246	the state that is already there. That is the same call a generated token
247	makes, and L7b's gate is that a sequence in chunks is the sequence whole.
248	
249	Measured on the second turn of a two-turn conversation: **90 prompt tokens, 71
250	of them reused, 216 ms against 421**. The log says which, per request.
251	
252	The reuse is all-or-nothing, and the reason is the gated DeltaNet. A
253	divergence part way through would mean rewinding to the fork — and the
254	attention cache is masked by position and both convolution rings are addressed
255	by it, so those would survive, but a DeltaNet layer's recurrent state is a
256	running product with no inverse. So the prefix has to be the whole of what is
257	held, or the sequence starts again. A miss costs one comparison; a hit costs
258	nothing and saves the history.
259	
260	It also means **the graph is one conversation's**. Two clients are served
261	correctly — the second waits, and re-prefills — but they take turns evicting
262	each other's prefix, which is the first thing a cache per conversation would
263	fix.
264	
265	## One prompt, three envelopes, and a template that is not ours
266	
267	The three chat endpoints are one generation. `/v1/chat/completions` is
268	OpenAI's, `/v1/responses` is OpenAI's newer one, `/v1/messages` is
269	Anthropic's, and each is a translation into the same `api.CompletionRequest`
270	and back out of the same token stream. Nothing but the envelope differs, which
271	is why the tests for two of them are about the translation and not about the
272	model.
273	
274	They do disagree about **reasoning**, and usefully. A chat completion carries
275	it in a `reasoning_content` field beside the content — not OpenAI's field, but
276	the one every client that talks to a reasoning model already reads. A response
277	carries it as an *item of its own*, before the message it led to. A message
278	carries it as a `thinking` block. All three come from the same place: this
279	checkpoint's generation prompt opens a `<think>` block, so the model's first
280	token is inside it, and `llm.ChatDecoder` splits the stream at `</think>` —
281	holding back any tail that could still be the start of a marker, so a `<` at
282	the end of a token is never forwarded as an answer and then taken back.
283	
284	**The prompt itself is a transcription and not a design.** A chat request is a
285	list of messages and the model reads one string, and what turns one into the
286	other is `tokenizer.chat_template` in the GGUF's own metadata: 180 lines of
287	Jinja that merge the leading system turns, add a reasoning-effort sentence,
288	write the tool block, keep each assistant turn's `<think>`, and open the
289	generation prompt. A server that improvises that produces a prompt the model
290	has never been shown — which does not fail, it answers slightly wrong,
291	everywhere, with nothing to point at. So `llm.RenderChat` reproduces it, and
292	the acceptance criterion is Jinja's own output: `reference/dump_chat_template.py`
293	renders the template out of the checkpoint with the environment transformers
294	builds, and `TestRenderChat` diffs 23 cases character for character. The cases
295	that made it worth doing are the small ones — Python's `json.dumps` writes a
296	space after every separator where Go's encoder writes none, and escapes
297	neither `<` nor `&` where Go escapes both, so the tool block was four
298	differences away from being someone else's prompt.
299	
300	**A stop sequence is another marker.** The same holdback that keeps
301	`</think>` from being forwarded half-written keeps the first character of a
302	stop sequence out of the stream, so a streamed answer and a buffered one are
303	the same string — the sequence itself appears in neither. They are watched in
304	the *answer* and not in the reasoning, because a `stop` of `"\n\n"` would
305	otherwise end every generation inside its own working. OpenAI's envelopes fold
306	this into `finish_reason: "stop"`; Anthropic's reports `stop_sequence` and
307	says which one matched, and so does this.
308	
309	**Tool calls are read back through the schema.** The template writes a string
310	argument raw between its tags and everything else as JSON, so rebuilding
311	`arguments` needs the tool's own parameter types: `123` is the number for an
312	integer parameter and the text `"123"` for a string one. They are also the one
313	thing that is not streamed — a call is not a call until it has closed, and a
314	client sent half of one would have to be told to take it back.
315	
316	## Transcripts have times in them
317	
318	Every emission the transducer makes records the encoder frame it was made at,
319	and a TDT model also predicts how many frames to skip afterwards — so a word
320	has an end as well as a beginning without a forced alignment. `verbose_json`
321	reports both granularities OpenAI defines, `srt` and `vtt` are the same
322	segments in their two containers, and `json` stays the text alone.
323	
324	Two things about them are worth stating rather than discovering. **The timings
325	are the model's own**: the duration head is approximate in a way a Viterbi
326	alignment against the audio is not, and 80 ms is the finest it can be. And
327	**Whisper's fields are absent rather than invented** — `avg_logprob`,
328	`no_speech_prob`, `compression_ratio`, `seek` and `temperature` are properties
329	of Whisper's decoder, and a number in them here would be a number a client
330	could filter on. `language` is likewise the request's or absent: this
331	checkpoint is multilingual and does not report which language it heard.
332	
333	Words are grouped by the tokenizer's own rule (SentencePiece's U+2581 marks a
334	word start) and segments are sentences, which this model can do because it
335	punctuates — a sentence end is a token rather than a guess about silence.
336	
337	## Extensions, and what is refused rather than faked
338	
339	`POST /v1/embeddings` takes an **`"instruct"`** field that is not OpenAI's.
340	Qwen3-Embedding is instruction aware: a *query* is meant to be prefixed with a
341	one-sentence description of the retrieval task and a *document* is not, and
342	the card measures 1-5% on downstream tasks for it. There is nowhere in
343	OpenAI's envelope to say so, so the field carries the task description —
344	`"instruct": "default"` asks for the card's own — and leaving it off embeds
345	the text as given, which is the document behaviour and the safe half. The
346	prefix is applied to the *text*, so it is inside the `usage` the response
347	reports. `"dimensions"` is honoured the way the card asks (MRL): the vector is
348	truncated and renormalised, so a 32-wide vector is still a unit vector.
349	
350	`POST /v1/audio/speech` takes a **`"phonemes"`** field that is not OpenAI's: IPA
351	to speak directly, winning over `input`. The checkpoint's vocabulary is 178 IPA
352	symbols and the front end that reaches them is a separate model's worth of
353	rules (SPEECH.md T5), so a caller that has already done that says so instead of
354	having it guessed. It is also how the endpoint is driven without a lexicon on
355	disk. `GET /v1/models` carries a **`voices`** array on the speech model, so a
356	client does not need a second call to populate a menu.
357	
358	Its **`"voice"`** also takes a *mixture*: `"af_bella,af_sky"` is the equal mean
359	of two style packs, which is not this server's invention — hexgrad's own
360	`KPipeline.load_voice` gives that spelling exactly that meaning, so the same
361	request is the same voice here as anywhere else kokoro runs (SPEECH.md T8).
362	`"af_bella:3,af_sky:1"` weights the mix, which is ours, and the weights are
363	normalised by their sum so they need not add up. Either every component
364	carries a weight or none does: `"af_bella:0.7,af_sky"` is a 400, because it
365	reads as either 0.3 for the rest or one share before normalising and a mix
366	that guessed would still sound like a voice. An unknown name is a 400 naming
367	*which component* was unknown, since that is the one thing a three-part string
368	does not tell you. The `voices` array stays the list of single names: a blend
369	is every comma-joined subset of them and not a list anything could enumerate.
370	
371	`POST /v1/images/generations` takes three fields that are not OpenAI's, and
372	each of them exists because the parameter is real here and there is nowhere
373	else to put it. **`"seed"`** names the initial latent's seed, and a response
374	reports the seed whether or not the request named one — a drawn seed that the
375	client is not told is an image that cannot be asked for twice. **`"steps"`**
376	is the denoising schedule's length, which is a host-side array and therefore
377	genuinely per request. And **`"aspect_ratio"`** — `"16:9"` and the like — is
378	fitted to the largest image *this* server holds, so a client wanting a
379	landscape picture does not have to know the ceiling to ask for one; `size`
380	wins when both are set, because that is the field every other server reads.
381	`GET /v1/models` carries an **`image`** object on the image model, alongside
382	the speech model's voices and for the same reason: `default_size`, `max_size`,
383	`size_multiple`, `default_steps`, `previews`, `max_partial_images`, `edits` and
384	`default_strength`, which are decided by what this process staged. The last
385	four are how a client finds out that `stream: true` and an edit will be
386	answered rather than discovering it from a 501.
387	
388	**Streaming an image** is OpenAI's `stream` and `partial_images`, and it needs
389	`-preview`. The frames are `image_generation.partial_image` — `b64_json`,
390	`size`, `output_format` and `partial_image_index`, plus a `step`/`steps` pair
391	this server adds so a client watching one arrive knows how much is left —
392	followed by one `image_generation.completed` carrying the finished image and
393	the `seed` and `steps` that produced it. There is **no `[DONE]` sentinel**:
394	these events are named, so the terminal one is already unambiguous, and the
395	sentinel exists on the chat endpoint only because its frames are not.
396	
397	Measured on one `-image -previews` process at 1024x1024, two runs each:
398	
399	| request | wall clock | first picture |
400	|---|---|---|
401	| no stream | 14.72 s / 14.80 | 14.7 s |
402	| `stream: true` | 14.76 s / 14.75 | 14.8 s |
403	| `stream: true, partial_images: 3` | **15.40 s** / 15.41 | **3.6 s** |
404	
405	So the framing is free and three in-progress frames cost **4.4%** — and what
406	they buy is a picture at 3.6 seconds instead of at fifteen. The frames land at
407	3.6, 7.1 and 10.7 s, from steps 1, 3 and 5 of the eight.
408	
409	Two numbers inside that 4.4% are worth separating, because only one of them is
410	the model. A preview decode is **87 ms** (`madebyollin/taef1`, IMAGE.md I2);
411	encoding the frame is the other **60**, and it would have been **344** at Go's
412	default PNG compression — four times the decode. Partial frames therefore go
413	out at `png.BestSpeed`, 15% more bytes for a fifth of the latency, while the
414	finished image keeps the careful encoder. A transient frame and a deliverable
415	are not the same object.
416	
417	**Which steps a partial comes from is the backend's decision**, not the
418	handler's: the step count may not have been named in the request, and how
419	finished a picture looks at step k is the scheduler's business. `backend`
420	spreads them evenly over *the steps that will actually run* and never takes
421	the last, whose denoised estimate *is* the final latent — a frame there would
422	be the finished image sent twice, once through each decoder. The "actually
423	run" is not pedantry: an edit at strength 0.5 runs the last four steps of
424	eight, and frames spread over all eight would every one of them fall before it
425	began.
426	
427	### Editing a picture
428	
429	`POST /v1/images/edits` needs `-image -edits`, and it takes **both encodings**:
430	`multipart/form-data`, which is what OpenAI's clients send and the only thing
431	their endpoint accepts, and a JSON body whose `image` is base64 (a `data:` URL
432	is fine), which is what curl and a test can write by hand. Both fill the same
433	struct.
434	
435	**What it does is SDEdit** (IMAGE.md I7): the picture is encoded to a latent,
436	the latent is mixed with noise at an intermediate point on the schedule, and
437	only the tail of the schedule runs. **`strength`** is how far back up the
438	schedule that point is and is the whole behaviour of the endpoint — near zero
439	returns almost the picture that was sent, 1 discards it and is an ordinary
440	generation, and the default is 0.8. It is an extension because OpenAI has no
441	such field: their edit endpoint is an inpainting model driven by a mask, which
442	is a different mechanism.
443	
444	Everything else is the generation endpoint's, including streaming, because
445	underneath an edit *is* a generation with a different starting latent. At
446	1024x1024 an edit is **cheaper** than a generation, and by exactly the steps it
447	skips:
448	
449	| strength | steps run | wall |
450	|---|---|---|
451	| 1.0 | 8 of 8 | 14.66 s — and bit-identical to a generation from the same seed |
452	| 0.8 (default) | 6 | **11.29 s** |
453	| 0.5 | 4 | 7.94 s |
454	| 0.3 | 2 | 4.63 s |
455	
456	The encode is a flat 430 ms of that, 3.6% at the default strength. A 512x512
457	edit over HTTP including the base64 body is **2.51 s**.
458	
459	**The size an edit with no `size` gets is the input picture's own shape**,
460	fitted inside the ceiling and rounded to a multiple of 16 — not the server's
461	default, which would silently reframe what was sent — and it is never scaled
462	*up*, because four times the tokens cannot paint detail the input never had. A
463	picture whose shape does not match the size being rendered is **cover-cropped**
464	rather than stretched, since an edit whose point is to keep the composition
465	should not begin by distorting it.
466	
467	What is refused rather than faked:
468	
469	- **`stream: true` on speech.** Kokoro decides the whole utterance's durations
470	  before a single sample exists, so there is nothing to send early. A whole
471	  body dressed as a stream would be a lie about latency.
472	- **`stream: true` on transcription.** The decode loop emits token by token
473	  and could stream, but the 40 µs submit-and-fence per emission is 38% of it
474	  (SPEECH.md), so what that endpoint wants is the persistent kernel, not a
475	  goroutine.
476	- **Containers other than WAV, and audio formats other than wav/pcm.**
477	  `audio/` is 16-bit PCM in and out on purpose. An mp3 request gets a 400
478	  naming what the server does encode. *Transcripts* are a different question
479	  and are no longer refused: `json`, `verbose_json`, `text`, `srt` and `vtt`
480	  all answer, because the timings they need exist.
481	- **`stream: true` without `-preview`.** It is a 501 naming the flag rather
482	  than a 400, because the request is well formed and the server was started
483	  without the decoder that answers it. With the flag it streams; see above.
484	  `/v1/images/edits` without `-edits` is the same answer about the encoder.
485	- **A `mask` on an edit.** A 501 that says what it would be rather than a
486	  picture that ignored it: a mask is blended into the latent at *every*
487	  denoising step, which is a mechanism and not a parameter, where `strength` is
488	  one number over the whole picture. More than one input image is a 400 for
489	  the same reason — OpenAI's field is a list because their model composites
490	  several, and this one does not.
491	
492	And on the chat endpoints, the same principle with a longer list: **`n > 1`**
493	(n completions are n runs of a model sized to saturate the device), **`min_p`
494	and `repeat_penalty`** (the sampler is temperature, top_k and top_p),
495	**`response_format` and `text.format`** other than text, a **`tool_choice`**
496	that names a function, **`thinking.budget_tokens`**, and any **image content
497	block**. Every one of them is a 400 that says what the server
498	does instead. The reason is the same each time: a knob accepted and ignored is
499	worse than a refused one, because the client never learns that turning it did
500	nothing.
501	
502	## Home Assistant speaks Wyoming, not OpenAI
503	
504	`-wyoming` opens a second listener on the same process: the two speech
505	backends over [Wyoming](https://github.com/rhasspy/wyoming), which is the
506	protocol Home Assistant's voice pipeline talks to a microphone and a speaker
507	with. It is a door and not a copy — one staging of the weights, one GPU
508	queue, one `models/` — so a request that arrives on 10300 and the same
509	request on 8080 are the same run of the same model. They are checked against
510	each other: the same text and voice through both produces byte-identical
511	samples.
512	
513	    In Home Assistant: Settings -> Devices & services -> Add integration
514	    -> Wyoming Protocol -> the host this runs on, port 10300
515	
516	One port carries both services. Wyoming's convention is 10300 for
517	speech-to-text and 10200 for text-to-speech, but a client discovers what is
518	behind a port by asking rather than by which port it is, so this answers
519	`describe` with both and Home Assistant creates an STT entity and a TTS
520	entity from the one entry.
521	
522	**There is no authentication, and there cannot be.** The protocol has nowhere
523	to put a credential: it is a framed JSON conversation over a bare TCP socket,
524	and every implementation of it assumes a trusted LAN. `-token` does not reach
525	this listener, and the startup line says so. That is why the flag takes an
526	address rather than a boolean — which interface it binds is the only control
527	there is, and it should be a decision somebody made.
528	
529	    13:03:47 wyoming: 1 asr, 1 tts (28 voices) as "strix-halo" on 0.0.0.0:10300;
530	             the protocol carries no credential, so -token does not apply to this port
531	
532	**28 voices, not 54.** Kokoro's packs cover nine languages and misaki's
533	English grapheme-to-phoneme is the one that is ported (SPEECH.md T5), so
534	`jf_alpha` over this protocol would be a Japanese voice reading English
535	phonemes. Over HTTP that is the caller's business, because
536	`/v1/audio/speech` also takes IPA directly and a caller with its own lexicon
537	is entitled to every pack; Wyoming has no phoneme field, so the default is to
538	advertise only what can be pronounced. `-wyoming-all-voices` offers the rest.
539	Each is described the way a menu wants it — `af_heart` is "Heart (American
540	English, female)" — and the name Home Assistant sends back is the pack's own,
541	so a blend still reaches `backend.TTS` by being spelled into it.
542	
543	**What it does not do.** Neither streaming direction is implemented, and both
544	are measurements rather than gaps: `supports_synthesize_streaming` would buy
545	the time between the first sentence of an answer and the last, and this part
546	synthesises nineteen seconds of speech in 162 ms (SPEECH.md T10), so the
547	whole utterance is ready before a satellite could have played the first
548	sentence of a streamed one — and kokoro decides an utterance's durations all
549	at once, so the pieces would have to agree about prosody they cannot see.
550	`supports_transcript_streaming` is the same shape at 257x real time. Wake
551	word detection, intent handling and satellite control are other people's
552	programs; `info` reports empty lists for them rather than claiming them.
553	
554	**The audio is converted where the protocol says it arrives, not where the
555	model wants it.** A `transcribe` stream declares its own rate, width and
556	channels, and this side reads 8-, 16- and 32-bit PCM at any rate and any
557	channel count and hands parakeet the 16 kHz mono it reads — through
558	`audio.Resample`, which is a filter and not an interpolation, because an ASR
559	front end with 80 mel filters up to 8 kHz treats aliased energy as a feature.
560	The HTTP endpoint still refuses a clip at the wrong rate, and the difference
561	is who is calling: there the caller chose a file and can convert it, here the
562	caller is a microphone. What is *not* converted is a stream that changes
563	format halfway through — concatenating two rates gives a clip whose timeline
564	is wrong in a way the transcript would not show.
565	
566	    wyoming[14]: resampled 3.25 s from 24000 Hz to 16000
567	    wyoming[14]: transcribe: 3.25 s of audio at 16000 Hz -> 44 characters,
568	                 in 23ms (140.4x real time)
569	
570	**A failure is an `error` event, not a hang-up.** Home Assistant reports a
571	closed socket as "connection lost" and reports an error event with its text,
572	so the difference is whether a misspelt voice shows up in the log as
573	`no voice "bm_geroge"; this checkpoint has 54` or as nothing at all. The
574	connection survives it: a client that asked for the wrong thing can ask
575	again.
576	
577	## What is left
578	
579	- **Constrained decoding**, which is the one refusal above that is a missing
580	  capability rather than a missing shape. It would close `response_format`,
581	  `text.format` and a `tool_choice` that names a function in one go.
582	- **More than one conversation at a time.** The graph is one sequence's, so a
583	  second request waits — and evicts the first's reusable prefix. What would
584	  change that is a cache per conversation and the residency to hold them,
585	  which is a measurement rather than an argument.
586	- **MTP speculative decoding** (LLM.md L9), which is the next thing worth
587	  1.5-1.8x on the endpoint that has just been wired.
588	- **Masked edits.** The encoder is ported and `/v1/images/edits` answers, so
589	  the mask is the only piece of that endpoint still missing: a blend into the
590	  latent at every denoising step, which is a mechanism rather than a
591	  parameter. Nothing in `GOALS.md` asks for it — the endpoint exists because
592	  OpenAI's surface does — and `strength` already covers editing the whole
593	  picture.
594	- **The image adapter holds the device lock for the whole run**, where the
595	  language model's takes it per forward pass. The same fix applies — between
596	  two denoising steps there is no work in flight — but it would mean the
597	  pipeline calling back out around every submit, and a step at 1024x1024 is
598	  1.7 s, so what a speech request waiting behind it would actually gain is a
599	  measurement rather than an argument.
600	- **`n > 1` images are serial**, and capped at four, because the device lock
601	  is. Four 1024x1024 images is a minute in one request.
602	- **A forced alignment** for the transcript timings, if the 80 ms grid and the
603	  duration head's approximation ever turn out not to be enough.
